---
title: "Cluster-randomized mediation (2-1-1)"
---

Chapter 9 reads a two-level `lavaan` fit in which treatment, mediator and outcome all vary within clusters. This
chapter takes the other common two-level design: the treatment is assigned to whole clusters (schools, clinics),
while the mediator and the outcome are measured on the individuals inside them, a "2-1-1" design. medfit fits it
with two linear mixed models from `lme4`, one for the mediator and one for the outcome, and keeps the result in a
`ClusterMediationData`. What this chapter shows is which terms of the outcome model the extractor reads, why the
indirect effect uses the between-cluster path, what the stored covariance leaves out, what the Kenward-Roger option
changes, and what the cluster bootstrap resamples. Each step is checked against base R: `lm()` on cluster means, a
within-cluster regression, a hand delta method, and a hand replay of the bootstrap draws. The user-facing page is
[Cluster-randomized trials (2-1-1)](https://data-wise.github.io/medfit/articles/model-cluster.html); the formulas shared
with the rest of the documentation are in
[Methods and Formulas](https://data-wise.github.io/medfit/articles/methods.html#cluster-level-treatment-the-2-1-1-design).

| | |
|---|---|
| **You need** | Chapter 5 (the delta method and the joint covariance); a mixed model with a random intercept (`lme4::lmer()`) |
| **You get** | the estimand and its split, how the paths are found by value, the oracles for the paths, the covariance blocks, the delta-method standard errors by hand, what `se_type = "kr"` changes, and the cluster bootstrap replayed by hand |
| **Time** | about 40 minutes |
| **Packages** | `lme4`; `pbkrtest` for the Kenward-Roger section. Without them the chapter's code chunks are skipped. |

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(medfit)
library(generics)
has_lme4 <- requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)
has_pbkr <- requireNamespace("pbkrtest", quietly = TRUE)
rd <- function(x, d = 4) round(x, d)
```

## The model and the estimand

For individual $i$ in cluster $j$ with cluster-level treatment $X_j$, write $\bar M_j$ for the mean of the mediator
in the cluster. The mediator model has a random cluster intercept $v_j$, and the outcome model splits the mediator
into its within-cluster deviation and the cluster mean, with a random cluster intercept $u_j$:

$$
M_{ij} = \beta_0 + a X_j + v_j + r_{ij}, \qquad
Y_{ij} = \theta_0 + c' X_j + b_W (M_{ij} - \bar M_j) + b_B \bar M_j + u_j + e_{ij}.
$$

The path $b_W$ is the effect of an individual's deviation from the cluster mean, $b_B$ the effect of the cluster's
mean level. Treatment moves whole clusters, and a shift of $a$ in every member's mediator moves the cluster mean by
$a$ and every deviation by zero, so the natural indirect effect is

$$
\text{NIE} = a \, b_B, \qquad \text{NDE} = c', \qquad \text{TE} = a \, b_B + c'.
$$

`decompose()` splits the NIE into an own part and a spillover part,

$$
\text{own} = a \, b_W, \qquad \text{spillover} = a \, (b_B - b_W), \qquad \text{own} + \text{spillover} = a \, b_B,
$$

and labels the split "cluster-average, large-cluster approximation": the exact own effect of one member depends on
the cluster size $n_j$, a point taken up below. The data in this chapter are simulated: 40 schools of 10 students,
treatment assigned by school, fixed seed.

```{r}
#| label: data
set.seed(2026)
n_cl <- 40
n_per <- 10
school <- rep(seq_len(n_cl), each = n_per)
x_cl <- sample(rep(0:1, length.out = n_cl))
v_cl <- rnorm(n_cl, sd = 0.5)
u_cl <- rnorm(n_cl, sd = 0.5)
dat <- data.frame(school = factor(school), X = x_cl[school])
dat$M <- 0.5 * dat$X + v_cl[school] + rnorm(n_cl * n_per)
mbar_true <- ave(dat$M, dat$school)
dat$Y <- 0.2 * dat$X + 0.3 * (dat$M - mbar_true) + 0.6 * mbar_true + u_cl[school] + rnorm(n_cl * n_per)
c(rows = nrow(dat), clusters = nlevels(dat$school), per_cluster = unique(table(dat$school)))
```

The engine route takes formulas with fixed effects only. It adds the random cluster intercept, the cluster mean of
the mediator and its within-cluster deviation.

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
x_fit <- fit_mediation(Y ~ X + M, M ~ X, data = dat, treatment = "X", mediator = "M",
                       engine = "lmer", cluster = "school")
class(x_fit)[1]
rd(paths(x_fit))
```

## Finding the terms by value

`extract_mediation()` on a pair of `lmer` fits does not look for a column called `M_cm`. It reads the outcome
model's fixed-effect design matrix and finds the three terms by their values: a column that is constant within
clusters and an exact affine function of the cluster mean of the mediator is the cluster-mean term; a column with
zero cluster means and an exact affine function of $M - \bar M_j$ is the within term; a column that varies within
clusters and is an exact affine function of $M$ is a raw term. The treatment and the intercept are never
candidates. The slope of the affine relation rescales the coefficient, so the names and the units of the columns do
not matter.

```{r}
#| label: extract
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
pair <- dat
pair$M_cm <- ave(pair$M, pair$school)
pair$M_cwc <- pair$M - pair$M_cm
fm <- lme4::lmer(M ~ X + (1 | school), pair)
fy <- lme4::lmer(Y ~ X + M_cwc + M_cm + (1 | school), pair)
x_ext <- extract_mediation(fm, model_y = fy, treatment = "X", mediator = "M")
c(extract_minus_engine = max(abs(paths(x_ext) - paths(x_fit))))
x_ext@parameterization
```

The engine route and the extraction route give the same paths. Two other ways of writing the outcome model reach
the same numbers. A raw mediator term next to the cluster mean, $b_W M + \kappa \bar M_j$, makes
$b_B = b_W + \kappa$, and the covariance follows by the linear map from $(b_W, \kappa)$ to $(b_W, b_B)$. A
cluster-mean column on another scale, here $10 \bar M_j + 3$, is found by value and its coefficient divided by the
slope:

```{r}
#| label: by-value
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
fy_raw <- lme4::lmer(Y ~ X + M + M_cm + (1 | school), pair)
x_raw <- extract_mediation(fm, model_y = fy_raw, treatment = "X", mediator = "M")
pair$M_cm10 <- 10 * pair$M_cm + 3
fy_10 <- lme4::lmer(Y ~ X + M_cwc + M_cm10 + (1 | school), pair)
x_10 <- extract_mediation(fm, model_y = fy_10, treatment = "X", mediator = "M")
keys <- c("a", "c_prime", "b_within", "b_between")
c(raw_param = x_raw@parameterization,
  raw_paths = signif(max(abs(paths(x_raw) - paths(x_ext))), 2),
  raw_vcov = signif(max(abs(x_raw@vcov[keys, keys] - x_ext@vcov[keys, keys])), 2),
  rescaled_paths = signif(max(abs(paths(x_10) - paths(x_ext))), 2))
```

Without a cluster-mean term there is no between path, and the extractor says so rather than guessing:

```{r}
#| label: no-mean-term
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
fy_no_mean <- lme4::lmer(Y ~ X + M_cwc + (1 | school), pair)
no_mean_msg <- tryCatch(
  extract_mediation(fm, model_y = fy_no_mean, treatment = "X", mediator = "M"),
  error = conditionMessage
)
no_mean_msg
```

## Oracles for the paths

When every cluster has the same number of members, the estimates of the mixed models are ordinary least squares
fits that can be written without `lme4`. The treatment coefficient $a$ of the mediator model is the coefficient of
`lm(M_bar ~ X)` on the cluster means. The outcome paths $b_B$ and $c'$ are the coefficients of
`lm(Y_bar ~ X + M_bar)` on the cluster means, and $b_W$ is the within-cluster slope of the deviations of $Y$ on the
deviations of $M$, since the deviation column is orthogonal to everything that is constant within a cluster. The
chapter-level function below is the oracle; it is exact here only because the clusters have equal size (with
unequal sizes the mixed model weights the clusters differently, and this chapter does not claim the identity).

```{r}
#| label: hand-paths
hand_paths <- function(d, cluster, y = "Y", m = "M", x = "X") {
  cl <- d[[cluster]]
  m_bar <- ave(d[[m]], cl)
  y_bar <- ave(d[[y]], cl)
  first <- !duplicated(cl)
  means <- data.frame(X = d[[x]][first], M = m_bar[first], Y = y_bar[first])
  a <- coef(lm(M ~ X, means))[["X"]]
  between <- coef(lm(Y ~ X + M, means))
  m_dev <- d[[m]] - m_bar
  b_w <- sum(m_dev * (d[[y]] - y_bar)) / sum(m_dev^2)
  c(a = a, b_within = b_w, b_between = between[["M"]], c_prime = between[["X"]])
}
by_hand <- hand_paths(dat, "school")
rd(by_hand)
```

```{r}
#| label: paths-oracle
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
paths_gap <- max(abs(by_hand - paths(x_ext)[names(by_hand)]))
paths_gap
```

The same identity covers the total effect. The reduced-form coefficient of the treatment in
`lmer(Y ~ X + (1 | school))` is $c' + b_B a$ by the omitted-variable identity on the cluster means, which is
`te()`:

```{r}
#| label: te-oracle
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
fy_reduced <- lme4::lmer(Y ~ X + (1 | school), dat)
c(reduced_form = unname(lme4::fixef(fy_reduced)["X"]), te = unname(te(x_ext)))
te_gap <- abs(unname(lme4::fixef(fy_reduced)["X"]) - unname(te(x_ext)))
```

## Own, spillover and the large-cluster approximation

The effects follow the formulas above.

```{r}
#| label: effects
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
tidy(x_ext, type = "effects", conf_int = TRUE)
dec <- decompose(x_ext)
dec
```

The own and spillover entries are the cluster-average, large-cluster limits. With the observed cluster mean, moving
only member $i$'s mediator by $a$ also moves the mean by $a / n_j$, so the exact effects in a cluster of $n_j$
members are

$$
\text{own}_j = a \left[ b_W + \frac{b_B - b_W}{n_j} \right], \qquad
\text{spillover}_j = a (b_B - b_W) \frac{n_j - 1}{n_j}.
$$

They add to $a b_B$ at every cluster size. The check below does not use these formulas: it shifts the mediator values
of one school in the outcome model's data and takes the difference of the fitted outcome predictions, once for a
shift of member 1 only, once for a shift of every other member.

```{r}
#| label: exact-own
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
a_hat <- x_ext@a_path
b_w <- x_ext@b_within
b_b <- x_ext@b_between
school1 <- pair[pair$school == "1", ]
n_j <- nrow(school1)
pred <- function(nd) unname(predict(fy, newdata = nd[1, ], re.form = NA))
base <- pred(school1)
only_member <- school1
only_member$M_cm <- school1$M_cm + a_hat / n_j
only_member$M_cwc[1] <- school1$M_cwc[1] + a_hat - a_hat / n_j
others <- school1
others$M_cm <- school1$M_cm + a_hat * (n_j - 1) / n_j
others$M_cwc[1] <- school1$M_cwc[1] - a_hat * (n_j - 1) / n_j
own_exact <- pred(only_member) - base
spill_exact <- pred(others) - base
rd(c(own_counterfactual = own_exact,
     own_formula = a_hat * (b_w + (b_b - b_w) / n_j),
     spillover_counterfactual = spill_exact,
     spillover_formula = a_hat * (b_b - b_w) * (n_j - 1) / n_j,
     sum = own_exact + spill_exact, nie = a_hat * b_b))
```

The approximation error of the own effect is $a (b_B - b_W) / n_j$; with unequal sizes `decompose()` uses the
harmonic mean $H$ of the cluster sizes, and it warns when this gap exceeds half the standard error of the own
effect. With ten members per cluster the gap is small beside the standard error, and no warning appears. With
clusters of three it is not. The simulated trios below make the between and within paths differ strongly:

```{r}
#| label: trios
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
set.seed(11)
n_trio <- 60
trio_id <- rep(seq_len(n_trio), each = 3)
trio_x <- sample(rep(0:1, length.out = n_trio))
trio <- data.frame(school = factor(trio_id), X = trio_x[trio_id])
trio$M <- trio$X + rnorm(n_trio, sd = 0.5)[trio_id] + rnorm(3 * n_trio)
trio_mbar <- ave(trio$M, trio$school)
trio$Y <- 0.2 * trio$X + 0.3 * (trio$M - trio_mbar) + 1.5 * trio_mbar +
  rnorm(n_trio, sd = 0.5)[trio_id] + rnorm(3 * n_trio)
x_trio <- fit_mediation(Y ~ X + M, M ~ X, data = trio, treatment = "X", mediator = "M",
                        engine = "lmer", cluster = "school")
trio_warning <- NULL
withCallingHandlers(
  trio_dec <- decompose(x_trio),
  warning = function(w) {
    trio_warning <<- conditionMessage(w)
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  }
)
gap_hand <- abs(x_trio@a_path * (x_trio@b_between - x_trio@b_within)) / 3
own_se <- sqrt(sum(c(x_trio@b_within, x_trio@a_path)^2 *
                     diag(x_trio@vcov)[c("a", "b_within")]))
rd(c(gap = gap_hand, half_own_se = 0.5 * own_se))
trio_warning
```

The warning is an advisory about the split. The NIE, the sum of the two parts, does not depend on the approximation.

## The covariance

The two models are fitted separately, so `@vcov` is built from the block-diagonal matrix of the two models'
fixed-effect covariances, $V = \operatorname{blockdiag}(V_M, V_Y)$, pushed through the linear map $T$ from the
stacked fixed effects to the four alias rows (`a`, `c_prime`, `b_within`, `b_between`) and each model's own
coefficients, $T V T^\top$. Every entry between the mediator block and the outcome block is set to zero by
construction: the covariance of $\hat a$ with $\hat b_B$ is not estimated, and it is not in `@vcov`. Entries inside
the outcome block are kept:

```{r}
#| label: vcov
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
V <- x_ext@vcov
alias <- c("a", "c_prime", "b_within", "b_between")
signif(V[alias, alias], 3)
cross_block <- V[c("a", grep("^m_", rownames(V), value = TRUE)),
                 c("c_prime", "b_within", "b_between", grep("^y_", rownames(V), value = TRUE))]
all(cross_block == 0)
```

The entry between `b_within` and `b_between` is near zero in this fit, since the within deviation is orthogonal to
the cluster mean. That is a property of this design, not something the class enforces; the entry between `c_prime`
and `b_between` is not zero.

### The delta method by hand

Every effect standard error is $\sqrt{g^\top V g}$ with $g$ the gradient of the effect over the alias rows. For the
NIE $a b_B$ the gradient is $(b_B, a)$ over $(a, b_B)$; for the own effect $a b_W$ it is $(b_W, a)$ over
$(a, b_W)$; for the spillover $a (b_B - b_W)$ it is $(b_B - b_W,\; a,\; -a)$ over $(a, b_B, b_W)$. The hand
computation below builds the quadratic forms from `@vcov` and compares them to `tidy()`:

```{r}
#| label: delta
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
grads <- list(
  nie = c(a = b_b, b_between = a_hat),
  own = c(a = b_w, b_within = a_hat),
  spillover = c(a = b_b - b_w, b_between = a_hat, b_within = -a_hat)
)
se_hand <- vapply(grads, function(g) sqrt(drop(t(g) %*% V[names(g), names(g)] %*% g)), numeric(1))
tidy_eff <- tidy(x_ext, type = "effects")
se_tidy <- stats::setNames(tidy_eff$std_error, tidy_eff$term)[names(se_hand)]
rd(rbind(by_hand = se_hand, tidy = se_tidy), 6)
delta_gap <- max(abs(se_hand - se_tidy))
```

## Kenward-Roger intervals

With few clusters the model-based standard errors can be too small, which is why the extractor warns below 25
clusters. `se_type = "kr"` asks `pbkrtest` for the Kenward-Roger adjusted covariance of each model's fixed effects
(`vcovAdj()`; it needs REML fits) and a denominator degrees of freedom for each path (`Lb_ddf()`), and the stored
`@vcov` is built from the adjusted covariances. Path intervals from `confint()` and `tidy()` are then t intervals,
$\hat\theta \pm t_{0.975,\,\nu}\, \mathrm{se}$ with the path's own $\nu$ in `@kr_df`. The effect intervals (NIE,
own, spillover, NDE and TE) stay normal.

```{r}
#| label: kr
#| eval: !expr has_lme4 && has_pbkr
x_kr <- extract_mediation(fm, model_y = fy, treatment = "X", mediator = "M", se_type = "kr")
x_kr@kr_df
rd(confint(x_kr))
```

The oracle for this section is again the cluster means. In this balanced data set the treatment effect on the
mediator is a two-group comparison of $J = 40$ cluster means, so a t interval on $J - 2$ degrees of freedom is its
exact form: the Kenward-Roger degrees of freedom of $a$ and the interval should equal those of `lm()` on the means.
The outcome paths $b_B$ and $c'$ are coefficients of a regression of 40 means on three columns, $J - 3$ degrees of
freedom, and $b_W$ is a within-cluster slope with $N - J - 1$:

```{r}
#| label: kr-oracle
#| eval: !expr has_lme4 && has_pbkr
means <- aggregate(cbind(M, Y) ~ school + X, pair, mean)
lm_a <- lm(M ~ X, means)
lm_between <- lm(Y ~ X + M, means)
n_obs <- nrow(pair)
rd(rbind(kr_df = x_kr@kr_df,
         oracle_df = c(a = lm_a$df.residual, c_prime = lm_between$df.residual,
                       b_within = n_obs - n_cl - 1, b_between = lm_between$df.residual)), 6)
rd(rbind(kr = confint(x_kr)["a", ], lm_on_means = confint(lm_a)["X", ]), 6)
v_adj <- pbkrtest::vcovAdj(fm)
v_model <- as.matrix(lme4::vcov.merMod(fm))
l_a <- matrix(c(0, 1), nrow = 1)
c(lb_ddf_a = unname(pbkrtest::Lb_ddf(l_a, v_model, v_adj)),
  var_adjusted = as.matrix(v_adj)["X", "X"], var_model = v_model["X", "X"])
```

Here the adjusted variance of $a$ coincides with the model-based one, so for the treatment path the whole difference
between `se_type = "model"` and `"kr"` in this balanced design is the t quantile in place of the normal one. That
coincidence belongs to this design and this path; the chapter makes no statement about how the two covariances
compare in general, and none about the coverage of either interval. The extractor warns below 25 clusters with
model-based standard errors, and below 10 clusters whatever the standard error type, and its message names the
remedies it recommends (`se_type = "kr"` where the model-based type is in use, and the cluster bootstrap).

## The cluster bootstrap

The effect intervals are normal approximations, and for a product such as the NIE the bootstrap is the alternative.
`bootstrap_mediation(statistic_fn, method = "nonparametric", data = , cluster = )` resamples whole clusters: it
draws $J$ cluster labels with replacement and stacks the rows of the drawn clusters in draw order. A cluster that is
drawn twice appears twice, and each draw gets a fresh cluster id before `statistic_fn` sees the data, so the repeated
cluster is refit as two clusters and not as one larger cluster. The interval is the percentile interval of the
replicates. A refit that errors, is singular or warns about convergence is dropped and counted in a warning.

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
dat_fit <- dat[, c("school", "X", "M", "Y")]
nie_of <- function(d) {
  unname(nie(fit_mediation(Y ~ X + M, M ~ X, data = d, treatment = "X", mediator = "M",
                           engine = "lmer", cluster = "school")))
}
n_boot <- 40
boot <- bootstrap_mediation(nie_of, method = "nonparametric", data = dat_fit, cluster = "school",
                            n_boot = n_boot, seed = 123)
boot
```

The percentile interval is the sample quantile of the stored replicates, and the replicates can be reproduced
without `bootstrap_mediation()`. The hand replay sets the same seed, draws the same $J$ labels per replicate,
relabels, and refits:

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-replay
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
set.seed(123)
values <- unique(dat_fit$school)
draws <- lapply(seq_len(n_boot), function(i) sample(values, n_cl, replace = TRUE))
replay <- vapply(draws, function(ids) nie_of(medfit:::.relabel_clusters(dat_fit, "school", ids)),
                 numeric(1))
c(replay_minus_stored = max(abs(replay - boot@boot_estimates)))
rd(rbind(stored = c(lower = boot@ci_lower, upper = boot@ci_upper),
         quantile = c(lower = unname(quantile(boot@boot_estimates, 0.025)),
                      upper = unname(quantile(boot@boot_estimates, 0.975)))))
```

The fresh ids matter. The same draw with the old ids keeps the distinct clusters only, so a cluster drawn twice is
counted once and the refit sees fewer clusters than the original sample:

```{r}
#| label: bootstrap-relabel
#| eval: !expr has_lme4
ids <- draws[[1]]
relabeled <- medfit:::.relabel_clusters(dat_fit, "school", ids)
kept_ids <- dat_fit[dat_fit$school %in% ids, ]
c(rows_relabeled = nrow(relabeled), clusters_relabeled = length(unique(relabeled$school)),
  rows_old_ids = nrow(kept_ids), clusters_old_ids = length(unique(kept_ids$school)))
rd(c(relabeled = nie_of(relabeled), old_ids = nie_of(kept_ids)))
```

## What the chapter does not establish

The oracles above check the arithmetic of the extraction, the covariance and the resampling against base R. They do
not establish coverage of any interval, the performance of the Kenward-Roger or bootstrap intervals with few
clusters, or the unequal-cluster-size behavior of the paths. The causal reading of the estimand (randomized
treatment, intact clusters, no interference between clusters, no unmeasured upper-level mediator-outcome
confounding for the NIE) is in `?ClusterMediationData` and the Methods article, and `medfit` computes the effects
without checking it.
